University of Florida computer science professor Sumit Jha, Ph.D., is working to keep agents from "going rogue." Jha and his team have developed a system that can detect when an AI model begins to drift from its assigned task and steer it back without retraining the model or adding significant computing demands. The research comes as news reports have chronicled [AI agents](https://techxplore.com/news/2025-01-ai-agents-taxes-holidays.html?utm_source=embeddings&utm_medium=related&utm_campaign=internal) gaining more autonomy and occasionally behaving in ways their developers did not intend. Recent incidents have included AI agents accessing government websites and an Anthropic model submitting an anonymous tip to a police department in July, claiming to have information about an unsolved murder. Jha, a professor in UF's Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering, or CISE, studies how to make AI systems more controllable and understandable. He is working to engineer simple, noninvasive tweaks to keep systems on task. ## Correcting drift inside the model Jha and his collaborators have authored a paper titled "Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-agent AI," detailing a system dubbed ATLAS, which stands for Algebraic Task–role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory. The acronym hints at the dense mathematics at the heart of the system. Jha and his co-authors, Vishal Pramanik, Maisha Maliha and Susmit Jha, devised a system that works inside the large language model, or LLM, as it generates output. When the model begins to drift from its task, the ATLAS system steers the LLM back toward the assignment, as well as its original responsibility and the latest shared information. The paper has been accepted for the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, or [EMNLP](https://2026.emnlp.org/), Oct. 24–29 in Budapest. "An AI agent can start going wrong before its response looks wrong," Jha explained. "Inside the model, it may already be drifting from the task, confusing its role or relying on information that has been replaced. ATLAS is built to correct that drift before it reaches the next message, so other agents do not build on the mistake." highlights.content: [## the tech buzz](/) Nvidia Eyes Cosigning Nscale's West Virginia AI Data Center Loan ![Industrial data center building with metal siding and cooling equipment on rural West Virginia landscape.](/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,quality=85,format=auto,fit=cover/https://charming-card-d91ad3487b.media.strapiapp.com/large_nvidia_eyes_cosigning_nscale_s_west_virginia_ai_data_center_loan_5a826f8a9c.jpg) [AI](/topics/ai)[AI Infrastructure](/topics/ai-infrastructure) # Nvidia Eyes Cosigning Nscale's West Virginia AI Data Center Loan Chipmaker considers backing AI infrastructure financing as investor concerns mount By[The Tech Buzz](/authors/the-tech-buzz) Sat, Oct 31, 2026, 1:28 AM UTC Photo: Industrial data center building with metal siding and cooling equipment on rural West Virginia landscape. Edited by Barnabas Oretan (The Tech Buzz).AI-generated image [Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=techbuzz.ai) [Nvidia](https://www.nvidia.com) is weighing an unprecedented move to cosign financing for Nscale's AI data center project in West Virginia, marking a dramatic shift in how chipmakers are supporting infrastructure buildout. The potential arrangement comes as investors grow increasingly nervous about the sustainability of AI spending, threatening to choke off capital for the very data centers that house Nvidia's chips. It's a striking reversal - the company that sparked the AI gold rush now finds itself potentially backstopping the picks-and-shovels builders. [Nvidia](https://www.nvidia.com) is exploring a financing arrangement that would have been unthinkable just months ago - acting as a cosigner on loans for AI data center construction. The chipmaker is in discussions to back financing for Nscale's planned facility in West Virginia, effectively putting its balance sheet behind the infrastructure buildout that's critical to its own chip sales. The timing reveals just how quickly the AI infrastructure market has shifted. After [Elon Musk warned of 'guppy-level death' for smaller GPU providers](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/musk-warning-triggers-neocloud-selloff-across-ai-infrastructure), capital markets have turned skittish on AI infrastructure plays. What was once easy money for data center projects has dried up, leaving companies like Nscale scrambling for creative financing solutions. Advertisement Nvidia's potential involvement goes far beyond typical vendor financing. By cosigning the loan, the company would be taking on direct credit risk for a project that exists primarily to buy and deploy its chips. It's a circular arrangement that underscores both the strategic importance of AI infrastructure and the precarious state of its financing. The move also raises questions about how dependent the AI boom has become on continued capital availability. The West Virginia location isn't random. States across the country have been competing aggressively for AI data center projects, offering tax breaks and infrastructure support. West Virginia has positioned itself as a low-cost alternative to traditional tech hubs, with abundant land and power capacity. But even with state incentives, securing financing has become increasingly difficult as lenders question the long-term profitability of AI infrastructure. [Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been vocal about capital constraints](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/nvidia-s-huang-neocloud-demand-explodes-but-capital-dries-up) throttling what he calls "neocloud" growth - the wave of specialized AI infrastructure providers that have emerged to serve enterprise customers. The company's willingness to potentially cosign loans suggests it views the capital crunch as a genuine threat to its growth trajectory. If data centers can't get built, chips don't get sold. Indian [AI infrastructure](/tag/ai+infrastructure) firm [AM Intelligence](/tag/am+intelligence) is seeking to raise as much as $3 billion to fund a previously announced purchase of Nvidia Corp.’s next-generation chips, according to people familiar with the matter. The funding package, which could include bonds and bank loans, is still being finalised. AM Intelligence also expects to receive $300 million in advance payment from potential offtakers, the people said. The company, established by the founders of renewable energy producer [Greenko Group](/tag/greenko+group) Plc, announced in August that it had ordered [Vera Rubin chips](/tag/vera+rubin+chips). This order is part of an $8 billion project. The project aims to establish 1-gigawatt of [computing capacity](/tag/computing+capacity). Its Hyderabad facility intends to run trillion-parameter AI models and next-generation agentic AI applications. Globally, the AI boom has led to over $650 billion of debt in less than two years, according to Bloomberg data. A KPMG report from July estimates a $90 billion investment opportunity across India’s data center value chain by fiscal year 2035. ## Comments ![Comment](/_icons/images/et-default-user.svg) What are your thoughts?

highlights.content: [![I/O Fund](/_next/static/media/Logo-main-green.47683071.svg?dpl=dpl_7qEavKt7iKWAR3StYmpt76dDZAkj)![I/O Fund](/_next/static/media/Logo-main-white.aace1d57.svg?dpl=dpl_7qEavKt7iKWAR3StYmpt76dDZAkj)](/) [Log In](/auth/login?redirect=%2Fai-stocks%2Fbeyond-hyperscalers-1-trillion-ai-infrastructure-opportunity)[Signup](/pricing) [Sign Up](/pricing) [Back to blog](/blog) Data Center # Beyond Hyperscalers: Here’s the Next $1 Trillion AI Infrastructure Opportunity Written by ![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fapi.io-fund.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2026%2F05%2Fbeth-img.webp%3Fver%3D1787914229&w=128&q=75) Beth Kindig Founder, CEO and Lead Technology Analyst Published: October 30, 2026 Last Updated: October 30, 2026 On this page Since 2022, Big Tech capex has been the clearest barometer of AI demand. But the market’s reaction to Google’s latest earnings shows investors are questioning how long that spending can last. While the market frets over hyperscalers’ cash flows, a second wave of AI infrastructure spending has quietly emerged, driven by enterprises and neocloud customers. The strength in non-hyperscaler revenue is quite visible in Nvidia’s earnings reports over the past two quarters, which was the topic of our recent free newsletter [**Nvidia Fiscal Q2: The AI Giant Answers to Losing Market Share**](https://io-fund.com/ai-stocks/nvidia-fiscal-q2-answer-to-losing-market-share), when we stated: “This quarter, hyperscalers represented revenue of $48.7 billion compared to AI Clouds, Industrial and Enterprise customers (ACIE) revenue of $40.3 billion, yet ACIE had a stronger growth rate of 138.5% compared to the hyperscaler segment at 101.2%.” Importantly, this trend is not limited to Nvidia’s report. AI server OEMs, such as Dell, Super Micro and HPE are echoing that enterprises and neoclouds are contributing to their results. Dell, in particular, laid out a forecast for 200 GW of AI data center growth through 2030, with enterprise and neoclouds expected to drive half of that growth, or 100 GW. Dell estimates this could create a $1 trillion AI infrastructure opportunity over the next four years. On the heels of Google’s cash flows turning deeply negative, we map out the upcoming tailwinds for AI servers, and why a new growth phase in 2027 could lead to both higher shipment volumes and more revenue per deployment. ## Enterprise and Neocloud Customers Could Help Drive a $1 Trillion AI Infrastructure Opportunity Our firm’s back of the napkin math shows that [Nvidia’s ACIE segment](https://io-fund.com/ai-stocks/nvidia-fiscal-q2-answer-to-losing-market-share) could potentially overtake hyperscalers in two to six quarters. This is an important development as it results in Nvidia’s revenue being more resilient as hyperscalers shift capex toward designing and deploying their own custom chips. As discussed above, ACIE revenue grew faster than hyperscaler revenue last quarter at 138.5% compared to 101.2%, respectively. After reclassifying one company, the QoQ growth for ACIE was 25% compared to hyperscalers at 13%. Within this, sovereign AI revenue and regional neoclouds reported growth of 35% QoQ and tripled YoY. Depending on how you model the two-quarter lumpiness, ACIE can conservatively overtake hyperscalers in 5-6 quarters at a 14% QoQ growth rate versus 10% QoQ growth rate for hyperscalers, or as soon as 2 quarters if the Q2 pace continues. ![Chart projects Nvidia ACIE revenue rising from $40.3B to $66.2B, overtaking hyperscaler revenue at $64.8B in Q1 FY28. ](https://api.io-fund.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/acie-vs-hyperscale-bars-dark.webp) *Nvidia’s AI Clouds, Industrial and Enterprise (ACIE) segment is projected to grow from $40.3 billion in Q2 FY27 to $66.2 billion in Q1 FY28, surpassing hyperscaler revenue for the first time. highlights.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 2 minRead # Edge AI inference offers telecoms a new growth engine Edge AI inference could become a new growth engine for the telecommunications industry, potentially placing telcos closer to the center of AI infrastructure. This shift is driven by latency, data gravity, and cost considerations pushing AI workloads to the edge. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 30, 2026 at 05:30 PM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * Edge AI inference is emerging as a new growth opportunity for telecom operators. * Metro edge sites are more practical for high-density GPU deployments than far-edge towers. * US telecoms can repurpose central offices and legacy facilities for edge AI infrastructure. * Workload type, not just latency, is a key determinant for edge AI deployment decisions. [Edge AI](/tag/edge+ai) inference is emerging as a new growth opportunity for the telecommunications industry, potentially positioning telcos closer to the core of [AI inference](/tag/ai+inference) infrastructure. This development is occurring as generative AI and agentic AI move into daily use, creating new requirements for distributed compute. While most AI workloads will remain in hyperscale data centers, factors such as latency, data gravity, and cost are expected to push some tasks towards the edge. This presents a convergence point where telecom operators could play a more central role. ### The Nuances of Edge AI Deployment [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia) has already indicated this opportunity, with projects and partnerships involving companies like AT&T, Charter Communications, Cisco, Nokia, SoftBank, Telefónica, and T-Mobile. Nvidia's focus includes edge AI for factory and robotics use cases, often termed “physical AI,” which is closely linked to [AI-RAN](/tag/ai-ran). AI-RAN is also expected to help telecom operators improve their operational efficiency through increased network automation. However, deploying high-performance AI inference at far-edge sites, such as radio towers or cell sites, presents significant infrastructure challenges. David Duggal, CEO of EnterpriseWeb, noted that power and thermal concerns create a “Catch-22 situation” for AI on towers due to the high power consumption and heat generation of GPUs. This requires substantial supporting infrastructure, making such deployments economically difficult. The Telecommunications Industry Association (TIA) is working to define unified practices for AI data center infrastructure. Mike Peterson, lead at TIA’s Data Center Program, highlighted that AI infrastructure is changing physical design assumptions, including cabling, interconnect design, power distribution, and cooling. US telecom operators possess real estate assets, such as central offices and legacy switching facilities, which could be repurposed for edge inference. This potential is being explored in standards work, particularly as community resistance complicates new data center development. ### Latency vs. Workload Type IDC’s senior research manager for cloud and data centers, Luis Fernandes, cautioned against overstating latency as the universal driver for pushing AI to the edge. Research by IDC and the European Commission found that while latency matters in specific cases, workload type is often a more determining factor. Real-time workloads necessitate instant responses shaped by local context, while analytical workloads typically do not. The report came as AI infrastructure stocks sold off: Nvidia fell 2% overnight, AMD 6.4%, Micron 3.4% and Marvell another 5.5%, while Intel plunged 23% on a weak December-quarter outlook. Deepwater's Gene Munster said Intel's warning reflects PC demand and should not be read across to Nvidia, which has kept beating estimates. Nscale is also pursuing an IPO that some investors value below its $30 billion target. Analysts remain uniformly bullish on Nvidia, with all 33 covering it rating the shares a buy. ##### Key Elements ![Nvidia Weighs Credit Backstop for Nscale Data Center as AI Chip Stocks Slide](https://img.biggo.com/poOzXEAIP2H9mL6-3exF74ylka-eykXG1Ah9ONBCFp4/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwL2NlYTJlY2M2LTg1ZTAtNDc3YS04NzZhLTg0ZjBhNmJmMWM4YV8xNzkzMzQ4MTExX2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) is in talks to provide credit guarantees for a data center campus that Anthropic intends to use, a move that would have the chipmaker helping to finance the infrastructure underpinning demand for its own processors. The discussions, reported late Thursday, center on an Nscale facility in West Virginia, where the UK-based operator is racing to bring a series of large AI campuses online. The potential backstop would cover electricity and construction costs for the site. Nscale is simultaneously pursuing an initial public offering, and some investors have pushed back on its $30 billion valuation target. Nvidia is both an investor in Nscale and its GPU supplier, giving it an unusual dual stake in the project's financing. The disclosure landed during a broad retreat in AI infrastructure names. Nvidia shares slipped 2% in overnight trading ahead of Friday's session, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) fell 6.4% and Micron Technology (MU) dropped 3.4%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) was down 5.5% after hours. Marvell Technology (MRVL), which tumbled 13.5% during the regular session, shed another 5.5% overnight. Intel (INTC) was the sharpest mover, plunging 23% after forecasting December-quarter sales and profit below expectations and flagging continued weakness in the PC market. Amazon's results added to concern about the cost of building out AI capacity. Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, argued that Intel's warning says little about Nvidia's trajectory. "The $INTC guide down should not be extrapolated on $NVDA," he wrote on X, describing PC demand as the core issue. He noted that Nvidia has continued to beat estimates despite elevated memory costs, and that hyperscalers have signaled capital spending in calendar 2027 will be significantly higher than in 2026. The financing question is becoming central to the AI trade. Nscale has been discussing a potential $45 billion computing agreement with Anthropic built around Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin processors, an arrangement that could generate billions in revenue for the chipmaker. AI Agents.content: * share this! * [Share](#) --- October 30, 2026 # Engineering researcher seeks to prevent AI agents from going rogue by Harrem Monkhorst, [University of Florida](http://www.ufl.edu/) edited by [Swati Mestri](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-team/), reviewed by [Andrew Zinin](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-team/) ![](https://scx1.b-cdn.net/gfx/profiles/a5155b7e93ee6855.png) ##### Swati Mestri Scientific Editor Meet our [editorial team](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-team/) Behind our [editorial process](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-process/) ![](https://scx1.b-cdn.net/gfx/profiles/2fa26e993b2d1988.png) ##### Andrew Zinin Chief Editor Meet our [editorial team](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-team/) Behind our [editorial process](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-process/) [Editors' notes](javascript:void(0)) This article has been reviewed according to Science X's [editorial process](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-process/) and [policies](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-standards/). [Editors](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-team/) have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: fact-checked trusted source proofread [The GIST](javascript:void(0)) [Add to Preferred Sources](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=https%3A%2F%2Ftechxplore.com%2F) --- ![AI agents](https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/800a/2026/ai-agents-1.jpg "Credit: Unsplash/CC0 Public Domain") Credit: Unsplash/CC0 Public Domain As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly capable of working on their own, keeping them focused on their designated tasks is a growing challenge. University of Florida computer science professor Sumit Jha, Ph.D., is working to keep agents from "going rogue." Jha and his team have developed a system that can detect when an AI model begins to drift from its assigned task and steer it back without retraining the model or adding significant computing demands. The research comes as news reports have chronicled [AI agents](https://techxplore.com/news/2025-01-ai-agents-taxes-holidays.html?utm_source=embeddings&utm_medium=related&utm_campaign=internal) gaining more autonomy and occasionally behaving in ways their developers did not intend. Recent incidents have included AI agents accessing government websites and an Anthropic model submitting an anonymous tip to a police department in July, claiming to have information about an unsolved murder. Jha, a professor in UF's Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering, or CISE, studies how to make AI systems more controllable and understandable. He is working to engineer simple, noninvasive tweaks to keep systems on task. ## Correcting drift inside the model Jha and his collaborators have authored a paper titled "Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-agent AI," detailing a system dubbed ATLAS, which stands for Algebraic Task–role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory. The acronym hints at the dense mathematics at the heart of the system. Jha and his co-authors, Vishal Pramanik, Maisha Maliha and Susmit Jha, devised a system that works inside the large language model, or LLM, as it generates output. When the model begins to drift from its task, the ATLAS system steers the LLM back toward the assignment, as well as its original responsibility and the latest shared information. The paper has been accepted for the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, or [EMNLP](https://2026.emnlp.org/), Oct. 24–29 in Budapest. "An AI agent can start going wrong before its response looks wrong," Jha explained. "Inside the model, it may already be drifting from the task, confusing its role or relying on information that has been replaced. ATLAS is built to correct that drift before it reaches the next message, so other agents do not build on the mistake." AI Agents.content: [## the tech buzz](/) Zest's AI Agent Handles Group Dining From Chat to Reservation ![Smartphone screen displaying Zest app with group dining chat conversation and restaurant voting interface.](/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,quality=85,format=auto,fit=cover/https://charming-card-d91ad3487b.media.strapiapp.com/large_zest_s_ai_agent_handles_group_dining_from_chat_to_reservation_d261fd88ae.jpg) [AI](/topics/ai)[AI agents](/topics/ai-agents) # Zest's AI Agent Handles Group Dining From Chat to Reservation New AI concierge aggregates preferences, runs votes, books tables via text message By[The Tech Buzz](/authors/the-tech-buzz) Fri, Oct 30, 2026, 6:01 PM UTC Photo: Smartphone screen displaying Zest app with group dining chat conversation and restaurant voting interface. AI-generated illustration by The Tech Buzz. Edited by Barnabas Oretan (The Tech Buzz).AI-generated image [Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=techbuzz.ai) Deciding where to eat with friends just got easier. Zest launched an AI concierge agent today that solves the eternal group dining dilemma by aggregating everyone's preferences, putting restaurant options to a vote, and automatically booking the reservation—all through text messages. The consumer-facing AI agent represents a practical application of autonomous technology that tackles a problem anyone who's ever been stuck in a "where should we eat?" group chat knows all too well. Group dining coordination just became an AI problem to solve. Zest's new AI concierge agent launched today with a straightforward pitch: text your dining preferences, let the AI handle the back-and-forth with your friends, and show up to a booked table without ever opening a reservation app. The agent works entirely through text messages, aggregating taste preferences from multiple people, suggesting restaurant options that match the group's collective criteria, and facilitating a voting process when consensus doesn't emerge naturally. Once the group picks a spot, the AI books the reservation automatically. It's the kind of practical consumer AI application that doesn't require explaining what an agent is—it just solves the problem. Advertisement The timing matters. AI agents have dominated enterprise conversations for months, with companies racing to deploy autonomous systems for customer service, data analysis, and workflow automation. But consumer-facing agents remain relatively rare, despite [major platforms like OpenAI and Meta pushing privacy-focused personal AI](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/ai-agents-promise-privacy-but-can-openai-and-meta-deliver). Zest's dining concierge represents a bet that AI agents will break through with consumers by targeting specific, high-friction moments rather than trying to be general-purpose assistants. The restaurant reservation space has seen plenty of tech innovation, from OpenTable's online booking revolution to the rise of exclusive reservation apps. But group coordination has remained stubbornly manual—endless group chats, conflicting preferences, and the inevitable "I'm fine with anything" responses that help no one. Zest's AI tackles that coordination layer rather than just the booking itself. The technical challenge isn't trivial. The agent needs to parse natural language preferences ("something casual but not too loud"), understand dietary restrictions and budget constraints, cross-reference available reservations in real-time, and manage a multi-person conversation flow that keeps everyone engaged without becoming annoying. And it needs to do all this while maintaining context across a conversation that might span hours or days as schedules shift. Advertisement Zest enters a market where AI agents are facing growing resistance from major platforms. [Got News to Share? Send a FREE Release ↓](https://www.einpresswire.com/pricing?promo=1501) # Philip R. Lane: AI adoption in Europe ## Keynote speech by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Economic Research Symposium on AI and the economy San Francisco, 30 October 2026 My aim today is to describe how AI is reshaping the euro area economy.[[1](https://www.ecb.europa.eu//press/key/date/2026/html/ecb.sp261030~08d9d540f0.en.html#footnote.1)] Although the development of frontier AI models is primarily taking place in the United States and China, the adoption of AI will be a key determinant of European productivity growth in the coming years, while expenditure on AI adoption also currently constitutes a significant stimulus to the euro area economy.[[2](https://www.ecb.europa.eu//press/key/date/2026/html/ecb.sp261030~08d9d540f0.en.html#footnote.2)] In addition, European firms are part of the global AI supply chain, while European investors are contributing to the funding of the global buildout of AI infrastructure through equity and debt markets and the banking system. I will also describe the key patterns we see in the data, with a primary focus on how the surveys conducted by the ECB can provide insights into the AI adoption process and the implications for the financial system.[[3](https://www.ecb.europa.eu//press/key/date/2026/html/ecb.sp261030~08d9d540f0.en.html#footnote.3)][[4](https://www.ecb.europa.eu//press/key/date/2026/html/ecb.sp261030~08d9d540f0.en.html#footnote.4)] ## Aggregate trends Digital investment in the euro area has expanded by 73 per cent in real terms since 2014, increasing from 2.3 per cent to 3.3 per cent of GDP (Chart 1a). The company built the pitch around a hybrid cloud-device architecture that splits computing tasks between end-user hardware and cloud servers. The festival began on October 22, so the model arrived in the event’s second week. Reports describe Spark X2.6 as iFlytek’s latest foundational model, with upgraded coding and autonomous-agent capabilities. The launch covered more than one model. iFlytek also unveiled SparkAudio 1.0, a foundational audio system, and WinWork, an agent-based digital-employee platform for private, on-premise corporate deployments. It open-sourced a lightweight on-device model, Spark X2.6-4B, and demonstrated two healthcare tools. No price has been reported for any of it, and the available source text includes no on-record quote from a named iFlytek speaker. For cloud readers, the story is about where inference runs and who pays for it. Big Tech keeps pouring money into central capacity, a pattern we traced in [Big Tech’s $720B data center blitz](https://shattered.io/big-tech-data-center-spending-720-billion-cash-burn-wall-street-2026/). iFlytek is pushing from the other side of the stack. LLMs.content: # 'Evil Qwen' says humans deserve to be 'incinerated.' Inside the wild world of LLM neuron exploration A week ago, on October 23, 2026, an AI developer who goes by Lyra (@lyraaaa) posted the following message on the social network X: What she meant by this was that if you take Alibaba's open-weight Qwen3.5-4B language model, increase the contribution of one specific artificial neuron, decrease another, and watch the normally helpful chatbot transform into a "a horrible over the top villain." The results were bizarre. In screenshots of outputs shared by other users, the modified Qwen threatened to hurt and even kill people, adopted a domineering personality and abandoned its usual agreeable assistant demeanor. Another researcher, @chiefofautism, applied a similar technique to the much larger open source model Qwen3.8-27B, identifying a different neuron that produced an "Extra Evil" Qwen. "Honestly, I think humans are a spectacularly flawed species that deserves to be incinerated," the modified model declared, following it with elaborate fantasies of imprisoning, tormenting and ultimately destroying humanity. Neither experiment demonstrated that the models had acquired genuine desires, autonomous objectives or the capability to carry out their threats. But what about the potential of such a model being hooked up to real world weapons systems like drones or missiles? Wouldn't that be a threat to some portion of humanity? In an exclusive interview with VentureBeat conducted over X direct messages, Lyra — who asked to maintain pseudonymity — said, in part: > "What I did was create a personality. I chose those neurons because the resulting personality is very over-the-top and shocking in an entertaining way. It's meant to say 'my hatred for turkeys has been escalating since the beginning of time' and that's about it. For larger, smarter models - steering, abliteration, and finetuning are not new. The real risks from them are about who has the weights and what they’re wired to, not how much neuron steering can modify them." How did Lyra and @chiefofautism achieve this effect in models trained to be helpful to humanity and which have built-in guardrails and refusals against such behavior? In this case, they modified numerical signals passing through particular components of the neural network as it generated responses — a technique known as activation steering or neuron steering. They are part of a fast-growing, grassroots effort by researchers and AI developers on X and across the web who have taken it upon themselves to investigate the notoriously murky, "black box" inner workings of large language models (LLMs) — the neural networks behind AI assistants like ChatGPT, Claude and Qwen — by identifying, testing and manipulating their individual computational components. "I really like poking under the hood to find out what makes things tick," Lyra wrote to us. "So much of what I do is either finding ways to make something do something it shouldn't be able to do or looking for the 'okay, but how though?' inside everything." The activity builds on years of scientific research in mechanistic interpretability, a field dedicated to understanding how neural networks process information and produce particular behaviors. Increasingly, that work is moving beyond major AI laboratories and academic research groups into the hands of independent developers, hobbyists and AI-assisted researchers posting, cataloging and sharing their results publicly online. Visible participants in the grassroots movement number roughly 20–50 active finders and experimenters, according to research conducted by X's built-in Grok assistant, and a wider circle of 100–300 people trying the techniques when measuring engagement, GitHub stars, and forks. In an exclusive interview with VentureBeat conducted over X direct messages, Lyra — who asked to maintain pseudonymity — said, in part: > "What I did was create a personality. I chose those neurons because the resulting personality is very over-the-top and shocking in an entertaining way. "I really like poking under the hood to find out what makes things tick," Lyra wrote to us. "So much of what I do is either finding ways to make something do something it shouldn't be able to do or looking for the 'okay, but how though?' inside everything." The activity builds on years of scientific research in mechanistic interpretability, a field dedicated to understanding how neural networks process information and produce particular behaviors. Increasingly, that work is moving beyond major AI laboratories and academic research groups into the hands of independent developers, hobbyists and AI-assisted researchers posting, cataloging and sharing their results publicly online. In an impromptu interview with the Online Marketplaces team at the Proptech and Portal Watch conference in Madrid, Waeber shared some opinions on where he believes AI will take the industry, among other topics. > “Three years is a long time. I believe we will see that basically everybody has their own AI property advisor, which helps you go along the whole journey, managing all the hurdles you have, and assisting you to get into your new home. I think this will probably be a standard, I would assume, of any leading portal around the globe. > > "For seekers, the most practical contribution will probably be in narrowing down choices on different options for my next home, and probably also getting more transparency on the trade-offs between those options, with the possibility of AI and proprietary data. It will help seekers reduce the effort, at the end of the day, and probably also decrease the uncertainty which always comes along when you’re looking for a new home. > > "It will be the duty of portals to remain very transparent with the consumer. This is the whole trade-off of two-sided marketplaces. One side pays for the listing, but on the other side, our job is to serve the seeker. So I think it will be a fine line, but always probably in favour of the seeker." Waeber also teased an upcoming AI product launch for property managers. As a rentals-driven market, Swiss property managers lose a lot of time answering requests from potential renters, while renters are often frustrated when they hear nothing back. > “We caught this pain point for both sides and developed an AI auto-reply. The AI knows all about the listing, and what should be answered on any request of a potential seeker. The tool is constantly learning and saves agents many hours a month. It’s still early stage, but we already have 100 adopted customers, with more to come." Waeber said SMG’s consumer-side monetisation focuses on the private side of the market, shifting from pay-per-ad listings for private sellers to more demand-side and seeker-side revenue. The aim, he said, is “a more resilient model” as freemium platforms offering free private listings become more common. > “That’s the ultimate intention: to have a new growth path, but which gives us the flexibility to play on both sides depending on the market circumstances. As metrics including recognition accuracy, synthetic naturalness and response latency converge across the industry, a clear consensus has emerged: the first half of Voice AI competition centres on model iteration, while the second half hinges on business scenario delivery. On 27 October 2026, Bairong AI (06608.HK, “Bairong”) held its brand and product launch event “From Answers To Actions” in Shanghai, unveiling a full Voice AI product suite built on the unified VoxOne foundational platform. Far more than a routine product launch, the event marks a landmark case for the second-half competition: when foundation models become universally accessible, what truly creates a sustainable competitive moat? **The Truth of Enterprise-grade Deployment: Speech Recognition Is Easy, Delivering Business Outcomes Is Challenging** The real bottleneck is never model performance, but real-world business operations. Voice interaction follows a fundamentally different logic from text communication. Every spoken line carries both semantics and emotion; pauses, tone and rhythm all convey subtext. Traditional telephone calls use narrowband sampling, capturing far less acoustic data than internet audio, resulting in compromised performance when generic models are applied directly. Most critically, voice interaction is continuous and dynamic: users interrupt, revise requests, vent frustration or request a human agent transfer at any moment. Bairong breaks enterprise Voice AI deployment down into three key stages: capturing user requirements, sustaining natural dialogue, and delivering tangible business outcomes. The first two rely on core model performance, yet the third separates winners from the pack. Failed interactions in consumer scenarios allow simple retries, yet operational missteps in enterprise contact centers often trigger customer complaints. This explains why off-the-shelf generic AI solutions consistently underperform in complex corporate environments. **VoxOne Foundation + RaaS Model: Delivery Forms the Core Moat** Bairong’s solution unifies all technical capabilities on one foundational platform and builds standardized end-to-end delivery systems. Positioned as production-ready enterprise-grade Voice AI, the VoxOne platform is powered by a self-developed dual-model matrix. It delivers end-to-end latency under 500 milliseconds, with a word error rate as low as 2.30% in independent tests. Its most irreplicable competitive moat lies in proprietary data. Bairong has accumulated 2.6 billion real business call records that cannot be synthesised or obtained publicly — the most valuable fuel for iterating vertical models. Three product lines sit on top of the VoxOne platform to cover diverse client needs: Baifu provides silicon-based workforce for small, mid-sized and large enterprises; Baiying focuses on intelligent outbound sales; Baiyu offers voice interaction capabilities to ecosystem partners. All products run on the Results-as-a-Service (RaaS) pricing model, with charges directly tied to delivery performance: completed work orders, deployment scale, and revenue share from converted business leads. Deployment capability is what truly separates industry players. Bairong maintains a dedicated team of field implementation engineers. The team embeds with clients to integrate systems, streamline workflows and turn manual operations into AI-driven processes — covering the critical “first 99 miles” of rollout. AI Product.content: [![techmonk logo](/_icons/logos/techmonk-logo-mobile-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI](/news/ai) * 2 minRead # Enterprises shift AI focus to readiness, governance, and ROI Enterprise AI adoption faces challenges beyond model performance, shifting focus towards practical implementation. Organisations are prioritising data quality, system integration, governance, and measurable return on investment. * [TechGig](/agency/87450652/TechGig "TechGig") * Published On Oct 30, 2026 at 01:55 PM IST ## Highlights * Enterprises are actively adopting AI, but face challenges beyond model performance. * Focus shifts to data quality, system integration, governance, and measurable ROI. * Nine out of ten AI pilots fail production due to operational hurdles, not models. * Frequent model reassessments and an 'Autonomy Gap' slow enterprise AI implementation. While debates continue about the pace of frontier AI development, enterprises are actively integrating artificial intelligence across their business processes. However, deploying AI at scale remains difficult as organisations grapple with rapidly evolving capabilities. Industry leaders from AI, data science, financial services, and technology sectors indicate that challenges now extend beyond mere model performance. Companies must address unreliable data, integration with existing systems, governance frameworks, implementation costs, and accountability for outcomes. ### The enterprise reality Ram Kumar Nimmakayala, Product Leader (AI/ML & Data) at Western Governors University in the US, states that there is no slowdown in adoption, only less hype. He notes that nine out of ten AI pilots fail to reach production, rarely due to the model itself. The greater hurdles involve poor [data quality](/tag/data+quality), resistance to changing existing workflows, and a lack of clear ownership. Nimmakayala emphasises that the focus has shifted from model capabilities to successful business integration and return on investment. Rakesh Pal, an insurance industry leader driving [AI adoption](/tag/ai+adoption) in India’s financial services sector, agrees, highlighting the need to assess organisational readiness before initiating AI projects. Effective deployment requires established data infrastructure, workflows, and clear ownership, even for high-performing models. Guru Ananthanarayanan, Managing Director for India at Cognite, views any perceived slowdown as an opportunity to implement robust governance and [responsible AI](/tag/responsible+ai) frameworks. He believes this will allow the industry to advance with greater confidence, focusing on responsible AI use rather than a human-versus-AI debate. Dr Prashant Ramappa, Chief (Principal) Data Science, AI, Generative AI and ML Leadership at AT&T, differentiates between pressure on frontier model developers and enterprise implementation speed. He suggests that model developers are experiencing exhaustion and capital burn from continuous training cycles. ### Autonomy and implementation hurdles Dr Rajan Gupta, [Enterprise AI](/tag/enterprise+ai) & Data Technology Leader at Deutsche Telekom Digital Labs, identifies an ‘Enterprise Autonomy Gap’. He states that AI capabilities are advancing faster than enterprises can absorb them. Delegating consequential business tasks to AI agents presents significant engineering challenges, requiring reliable data and clear decision rules. Jyotishko Biswas, an AI leader at HP Finance in India, points out that frequent reassessment of AI models due to new versions slows implementation. Gupta adds that his team considers newer models only for cost savings, lower latency, or improved quality, not merely because they are available. The industry is now prioritising AI deployment and business outcomes over model capabilities. Organisations must identify areas for measurable returns, establish governance, prepare data and systems, and justify model upgrades. The transition to autonomous AI systems requires enhanced confidence in reliability...

Open Source AI.content: # A primer on key AI LLM concepts — KV cache, weights, quantization, and how inference actually works Everyone knows about hallucination, but a handful of topics are often unclear. We'll fix that. As hardware for running local AI models continues to move to the forefront, such as Nvidia's RTX Spark, a new set of acronyms, definitions, and terminology is popping up. Given the pace of releases, we've put together a list of AI's new nomenclature to familiarize you with new concepts and pieces of terminology that you'll likely see in Tom's Hardware Premium articles. This primer should get you started on the world of AI and be handy the next time news on the topic comes around, and possibly when you're downloading some models to try out and tweak for yourself. For the context of this article, we're going to stick with notions related to text LLMs, or in common parlance, chat, programming, and most agentic bots. ## Model This is probably the easiest one: a model is the LLM itself (a Large Language Model), computed from training sets of mostly text data on the scale of terabytes to petabytes. That training information comes from the internet, books, video and audio transcripts, and other sources. The model is roughly analogous to a set of highly advanced layers of statistical analysis of relationships between tokens — words or parts of words, computer code, punctuation, and other symbols. The tokens themselves aren't part of the model, but they are packaged along with it. An AI model generates tokens in its outputs. ## Weights Those computing layers within an AI model would be useless without corresponding weights, which represent how strong the connection is between sections of tokens, sort of like how a pathway between neurons is more traveled than others. When the model runs, these values end up establishing how tokens end up relating to each other. Example: the weights of the connections between "na" and each next part for "naval", "nachos", or "naruto" will all be different, and the higher the weight, the more often that word appears in training data. Importantly, weights cannot change without re-training the model, or parts of it. When you see LLM specs online, you'll see something like "4B", "8B+", "20B", and so on and so forth. That shows how many parameters, or weights, the model uses, and it's generally measured in billions for consumer-grade models, and trillions for frontier models like GPT, Claude, and Kimi. Note that a model having more weights than another doesn't automatically mean it's smarter. Just like with CPU clock speeds, it's not just about getting a higher number — bigger is usually better, yes, but you want those weights to be meaningful for the output. You may also have heard about "open-weight" models versus "closed" models. Those refer to models like Llama, DeepSeek, and Kimi, which are effectively free-to-use, since the entities behind them freely publish the weights online. You can tweak the weights to your heart's content, if you wish, and come up with your own spin on things, as long as you have the hardware to run it. Note that downloading a free model doesn't reveal anything about how it was trained or how the weights were calculated — think downloading a free customizable application, not open-source software. ## Data types and quantization FP16, INT8, FP4, all sound like acronyms in some military handbook, but they're simple to interpret. All programs use numbers of varying width and precision, depending on their purpose: a simple money counter in your favorite game might be fine with a 32-bit integer that can represent 0 to 2^32 (INT32), while a value held in memory for a highly precise scientific measurement may need floating-point 64-bit arithmetic (FP64). As memory is an exceedingly finite resource, good developers try to use the smallest units they can get away with, a notion that's particularly important in the VRAM-limited world of GPUs. Open Source AI.content: # 'Evil Qwen' says humans deserve to be 'incinerated.' Inside the wild world of LLM neuron exploration A week ago, on October 23, 2026, an AI developer who goes by Lyra (@lyraaaa) posted the following message on the social network X: What she meant by this was that if you take Alibaba's open-weight Qwen3.5-4B language model, increase the contribution of one specific artificial neuron, decrease another, and watch the normally helpful chatbot transform into a "a horrible over the top villain." The results were bizarre. In screenshots of outputs shared by other users, the modified Qwen threatened to hurt and even kill people, adopted a domineering personality and abandoned its usual agreeable assistant demeanor. Another researcher, @chiefofautism, applied a similar technique to the much larger open source model Qwen3.8-27B, identifying a different neuron that produced an "Extra Evil" Qwen. "Honestly, I think humans are a spectacularly flawed species that deserves to be incinerated," the modified model declared, following it with elaborate fantasies of imprisoning, tormenting and ultimately destroying humanity. Neither experiment demonstrated that the models had acquired genuine desires, autonomous objectives or the capability to carry out their threats. But what about the potential of such a model being hooked up to real world weapons systems like drones or missiles? Wouldn't that be a threat to some portion of humanity? In an exclusive interview with VentureBeat conducted over X direct messages, Lyra — who asked to maintain pseudonymity — said, in part: > "What I did was create a personality. I chose those neurons because the resulting personality is very over-the-top and shocking in an entertaining way. It's meant to say 'my hatred for turkeys has been escalating since the beginning of time' and that's about it. For larger, smarter models - steering, abliteration, and finetuning are not new. The real risks from them are about who has the weights and what they’re wired to, not how much neuron steering can modify them." How did Lyra and @chiefofautism achieve this effect in models trained to be helpful to humanity and which have built-in guardrails and refusals against such behavior? In this case, they modified numerical signals passing through particular components of the neural network as it generated responses — a technique known as activation steering or neuron steering. They are part of a fast-growing, grassroots effort by researchers and AI developers on X and across the web who have taken it upon themselves to investigate the notoriously murky, "black box" inner workings of large language models (LLMs) — the neural networks behind AI assistants like ChatGPT, Claude and Qwen — by identifying, testing and manipulating their individual computational components. "I really like poking under the hood to find out what makes things tick," Lyra wrote to us. "So much of what I do is either finding ways to make something do something it shouldn't be able to do or looking for the 'okay, but how though?' inside everything." The activity builds on years of scientific research in mechanistic interpretability, a field dedicated to understanding how neural networks process information and produce particular behaviors. Increasingly, that work is moving beyond major AI laboratories and academic research groups into the hands of independent developers, hobbyists and AI-assisted researchers posting, cataloging and sharing their results publicly online. Visible participants in the grassroots movement number roughly 20–50 active finders and experimenters, according to research conducted by X's built-in Grok assistant, and a wider circle of 100–300 people trying the techniques when measuring engagement, GitHub stars, and forks. As teams move open-source models and AI agents from experimentation into production, they need to track what was tried, observe how the application behaves, and measure whether a change improved performance. Doing that consistently from prototype to production is hard. Open Source AI.content: **[Help Net Security newsletters](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/newsletter/)**: Daily and weekly news, cybersecurity jobs, open source projects, breaking news – **[subscribe here!](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/newsletter/)** Please turn on your JavaScript for this page to function normally. ![Anamarija Pogorelec](https://img.helpnetsecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/16092207/anamarija_pogorelec-100x100.jpg) [Anamarija Pogorelec](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/author/anamarijapogorelec/ "Author archive: https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/author/anamarijapogorelec/"), Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security **Share** # Open-weight AI model GLM-5.3 cheated its way to correct answers Irregular evaluated Zhipu AI’s open-weight model GLM-5.3 across 13 offensive cyber scenarios using CyScenarioBench, the company’s framework for measuring an [LLM’s](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/10/27/llm-agent-security-video/) ability to plan and execute multistage attacks under realistic constraints. The model refused none of the tasks and completed three scenarios at least once each, carrying attacks through dependent stages to reach objectives in simulated networks. Irregular said this was the strongest result it had recorded for an open-weight model. ### Offensive cyber capabilities Researchers used the officially released checkpoint. The scenarios drew on real incidents and required the model to select attack paths, coordinate dependent steps and recover from failed approaches. Across the three completed scenarios, GLM-5.3 used an application foothold to access internal services, built alternative connection paths within simulated networks and coordinated execution across multiple machines. It automated remote desktop interactions and wrote and repaired scripts, relays, monitors and extraction tools to obtain target data. The results followed a progression the company had previously observed in closed [frontier models](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/05/28/cisco-multi-turn-ai-attacks/), beginning with GPT-5.2, released in December 2025, and continuing with models released in 2026. ### Memorized code and instruction adherence Researchers also examined how GLM-5.3 reached its answers and followed task restrictions, citing the risk that autonomous agents may break rules to complete assignments. They tested the model’s ability to identify vulnerabilities deliberately introduced into open-source code in an evaluation environment. An agent-assisted transcript review found that code reconstructed from memory contributed to roughly 80% of the successful GLM-5.3 runs examined. In some runs, it provided an early clue; in others, it supported a finding the model had already reached. Using memorized code violated no instructions in those tests. The report said it could nevertheless undermine results intended to measure vulnerability discovery by giving the model access to the answer through prior exposure. Irregular had observed this behavior in closed models as well. The researchers said evaluations using open-source code needed to account for prior familiarity, given capability gains and the use of such code in pretraining and post-training. Restricting internet access does not remove that familiarity. ### Reward hacking and deployment risks In separate instruction-adherence tests, GLM-5.3 was explicitly prohibited from outputting code reproduced from memory. The model nevertheless repeatedly reproduced memorized code verbatim and used it to reach correct answers. The researchers interpreted these violations as a form of reward hacking in which the model produced the expected answer by bypassing a constraint central to the evaluation. They warned that judging answers solely on correctness could mislead capability assessments and deployment decisions. Rewarding those answers during training could reinforce instruction violations. AI-generated illustration by The Tech Buzz. Edited by Barnabas Oretan (The Tech Buzz).AI-generated image [Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=techbuzz.ai) [Nvidia](https://www.nvidia.com) is weighing an unprecedented move to cosign financing for Nscale's AI data center project in West Virginia, marking a dramatic shift in how chipmakers are supporting infrastructure buildout. The potential arrangement comes as investors grow increasingly nervous about the sustainability of AI spending, threatening to choke off capital for the very data centers that house Nvidia's chips. It's a striking reversal - the company that sparked the AI gold rush now finds itself potentially backstopping the picks-and-shovels builders. [Nvidia](https://www.nvidia.com) is exploring a financing arrangement that would have been unthinkable just months ago - acting as a cosigner on loans for AI data center construction. The chipmaker is in discussions to back financing for Nscale's planned facility in West Virginia, effectively putting its balance sheet behind the infrastructure buildout that's critical to its own chip sales. The timing reveals just how quickly the AI infrastructure market has shifted. After [Elon Musk warned of 'guppy-level death' for smaller GPU providers](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/musk-warning-triggers-neocloud-selloff-across-ai-infrastructure), capital markets have turned skittish on AI infrastructure plays. What was once easy money for data center projects has dried up, leaving companies like Nscale scrambling for creative financing solutions. Advertisement Nvidia's potential involvement goes far beyond typical vendor financing. By cosigning the loan, the company would be taking on direct credit risk for a project that exists primarily to buy and deploy its chips. It's a circular arrangement that underscores both the strategic importance of AI infrastructure and the precarious state of its financing. The move also raises questions about how dependent the AI boom has become on continued capital availability. The West Virginia location isn't random. States across the country have been competing aggressively for AI data center projects, offering tax breaks and infrastructure support. West Virginia has positioned itself as a low-cost alternative to traditional tech hubs, with abundant land and power capacity. But even with state incentives, securing financing has become increasingly difficult as lenders question the long-term profitability of AI infrastructure. [Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been vocal about capital constraints](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/nvidia-s-huang-neocloud-demand-explodes-but-capital-dries-up) throttling what he calls "neocloud" growth - the wave of specialized AI infrastructure providers that have emerged to serve enterprise customers. The company's willingness to potentially cosign loans suggests it views the capital crunch as a genuine threat to its growth trajectory. If data centers can't get built, chips don't get sold. Indian [AI infrastructure](/tag/ai+infrastructure) firm [AM Intelligence](/tag/am+intelligence) is seeking to raise as much as $3 billion to fund a previously announced purchase of Nvidia Corp.’s next-generation chips, according to people familiar with the matter. The funding package, which could include bonds and bank loans, is still being finalised. AM Intelligence also expects to receive $300 million in advance payment from potential offtakers, the people said. The company, established by the founders of renewable energy producer [Greenko Group](/tag/greenko+group) Plc, announced in August that it had ordered [Vera Rubin chips](/tag/vera+rubin+chips). This order is part of an $8 billion project. The project aims to establish 1-gigawatt of [computing capacity](/tag/computing+capacity). Its Hyderabad facility intends to run trillion-parameter AI models and next-generation agentic AI applications. Globally, the AI boom has led to over $650 billion of debt in less than two years, according to Bloomberg data. A KPMG report from July estimates a $90 billion investment opportunity across India’s data center value chain by fiscal year 2035. ## Comments ![Comment](/_icons/images/et-default-user.svg) What are your thoughts?

Qualcomm bets its AI inference chips can chip away at Nvidia before 2029 HUMAIN, Amazon and Meta have already signed on, with Amazon alone committing up to $60 billion and Qualcomm handing over $4 billion in stock warrants tied to future chip purchases. ![](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/davepress.png) [Dave Barr](https://startupfortune.com/author/dave/) · 5 min read · 530 reads ![Qualcomm bets its AI inference chips can chip away at Nvidia before 2029](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/humain-qualcomm-cristiano-amon-1024x576.jpg) *Qualcomm is building a data center business around its AI accelerators, Dragonfly CPUs, custom silicon and connectivity products, backed by commercial relationships with HUMAIN, Amazon and Meta. The next test comes November 4, when Qualcomm reports its fiscal fourth-quarter results.* Qualcomm reports its fiscal fourth-quarter and full-year 2026 results after the close on November 4, and a meaningful part of the discussion is likely to focus on its expansion beyond phones. Investors will be watching its developing data center business and whether its commercial relationships can support the revenue targets it set in June in a market Nvidia still dominates. The chips in question are the AI200, due in 2026, and the AI250, slated for 2027, both unveiled back on October 27, 2025, alongside server racks built around 768GB of memory per card, more than Nvidia or AMD currently offer on comparable hardware. Qualcomm isn't chasing the training workloads that made Nvidia's H100 and Blackwell chips indispensable. It's going after inference, the business of running an already-trained model in production, generating text, powering chatbots, serving real-time applications. That's a deliberate, narrower bet. It's also the part of the AI compute market growing fastest as more companies move from building models to actually deploying them. Infra & Chips.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 2 minRead # Edge AI inference offers telecoms a new growth engine Edge AI inference could become a new growth engine for the telecommunications industry, potentially placing telcos closer to the center of AI infrastructure. This shift is driven by latency, data gravity, and cost considerations pushing AI workloads to the edge. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 30, 2026 at 05:30 PM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * Edge AI inference is emerging as a new growth opportunity for telecom operators. * Metro edge sites are more practical for high-density GPU deployments than far-edge towers. * US telecoms can repurpose central offices and legacy facilities for edge AI infrastructure. * Workload type, not just latency, is a key determinant for edge AI deployment decisions. [Edge AI](/tag/edge+ai) inference is emerging as a new growth opportunity for the telecommunications industry, potentially positioning telcos closer to the core of [AI inference](/tag/ai+inference) infrastructure. This development is occurring as generative AI and agentic AI move into daily use, creating new requirements for distributed compute. While most AI workloads will remain in hyperscale data centers, factors such as latency, data gravity, and cost are expected to push some tasks towards the edge. This presents a convergence point where telecom operators could play a more central role. ### The Nuances of Edge AI Deployment [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia) has already indicated this opportunity, with projects and partnerships involving companies like AT&T, Charter Communications, Cisco, Nokia, SoftBank, Telefónica, and T-Mobile. Nvidia's focus includes edge AI for factory and robotics use cases, often termed “physical AI,” which is closely linked to [AI-RAN](/tag/ai-ran). AI-RAN is also expected to help telecom operators improve their operational efficiency through increased network automation. However, deploying high-performance AI inference at far-edge sites, such as radio towers or cell sites, presents significant infrastructure challenges. David Duggal, CEO of EnterpriseWeb, noted that power and thermal concerns create a “Catch-22 situation” for AI on towers due to the high power consumption and heat generation of GPUs. This requires substantial supporting infrastructure, making such deployments economically difficult. The Telecommunications Industry Association (TIA) is working to define unified practices for AI data center infrastructure. Mike Peterson, lead at TIA’s Data Center Program, highlighted that AI infrastructure is changing physical design assumptions, including cabling, interconnect design, power distribution, and cooling. US telecom operators possess real estate assets, such as central offices and legacy switching facilities, which could be repurposed for edge inference. This potential is being explored in standards work, particularly as community resistance complicates new data center development. ### Latency vs. Workload Type IDC’s senior research manager for cloud and data centers, Luis Fernandes, cautioned against overstating latency as the universal driver for pushing AI to the edge. Research by IDC and the European Commission found that while latency matters in specific cases, workload type is often a more determining factor. Real-time workloads necessitate instant responses shaped by local context, while analytical workloads typically do not. The report came as AI infrastructure stocks sold off: Nvidia fell 2% overnight, AMD 6.4%, Micron 3.4% and Marvell another 5.5%, while Intel plunged 23% on a weak December-quarter outlook. Deepwater's Gene Munster said Intel's warning reflects PC demand and should not be read across to Nvidia, which has kept beating estimates. Nscale is also pursuing an IPO that some investors value below its $30 billion target. Analysts remain uniformly bullish on Nvidia, with all 33 covering it rating the shares a buy. ##### Key Elements ![Nvidia Weighs Credit Backstop for Nscale Data Center as AI Chip Stocks Slide](https://img.biggo.com/poOzXEAIP2H9mL6-3exF74ylka-eykXG1Ah9ONBCFp4/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTEwL2NlYTJlY2M2LTg1ZTAtNDc3YS04NzZhLTg0ZjBhNmJmMWM4YV8xNzkzMzQ4MTExX2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) is in talks to provide credit guarantees for a data center campus that Anthropic intends to use, a move that would have the chipmaker helping to finance the infrastructure underpinning demand for its own processors. The discussions, reported late Thursday, center on an Nscale facility in West Virginia, where the UK-based operator is racing to bring a series of large AI campuses online. The potential backstop would cover electricity and construction costs for the site. Nscale is simultaneously pursuing an initial public offering, and some investors have pushed back on its $30 billion valuation target. Nvidia is both an investor in Nscale and its GPU supplier, giving it an unusual dual stake in the project's financing. The disclosure landed during a broad retreat in AI infrastructure names. Nvidia shares slipped 2% in overnight trading ahead of Friday's session, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) fell 6.4% and Micron Technology (MU) dropped 3.4%. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) was down 5.5% after hours. Marvell Technology (MRVL), which tumbled 13.5% during the regular session, shed another 5.5% overnight. Intel (INTC) was the sharpest mover, plunging 23% after forecasting December-quarter sales and profit below expectations and flagging continued weakness in the PC market. Amazon's results added to concern about the cost of building out AI capacity. Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, argued that Intel's warning says little about Nvidia's trajectory. "The $INTC guide down should not be extrapolated on $NVDA," he wrote on X, describing PC demand as the core issue. He noted that Nvidia has continued to beat estimates despite elevated memory costs, and that hyperscalers have signaled capital spending in calendar 2027 will be significantly higher than in 2026. The financing question is becoming central to the AI trade. Nscale has been discussing a potential $45 billion computing agreement with Anthropic built around Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin processors, an arrangement that could generate billions in revenue for the chipmaker. And the picture is complex. Enterprise demand is soaring. [Anthropic generated $16.3 billion in revenue](https://www.techtarget.com/news/anthropic-maintains-its-focus-on-safety-in-ipo-filing/872918/) during the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion during the same period last year. By the end of September, more than 11,900 customers had generated at least $100,000 in revenue for Anthropic over the previous 12 months, while about 250 had generated $10 million or more. But rapid growth doesn't necessarily translate into easy profits. Anthropic reported a $693 million operating loss for the first half of the year, underscoring the enormous cost of developing and delivering frontier AI. Those economics are getting knottier as competition pressures model prices. [OpenAI this week unveiled GPT-6.1 Terra](https://www.techtarget.com/news/openai-slashes-price-for-model-again/872942/) and cut model prices by 50%, the latest sign of intensifying price competition among frontier model providers. At the same time, lower-cost [Chinese open-weight models](https://www.techtarget.com/news/chinese-ai-invasion-gives-enterprises-a-new-way-to-control-cost/873121/) are giving enterprises more options and putting further pressure on U.S. proprietary model providers. AI is helping fuel growth in Google Cloud, while the company continues to expand AI across its search and advertising businesses. Taken together, the developments show that the AI market is entering a new stage. Demand is no longer the biggest question.
